title: Start in order and stay up
intro: An application made of several containers has to start in a workable order, recover when a part fails, and not take the whole machine down when a part misbehaves. This module covers health checks, waiting for a dependency to be ready, restart policies and resource limits.

steps.title: Started is not ready
steps.text:
`depends_on` in its short form makes Compose start the database container before the web container. It does not wait for the database to be **ready**.

A database needs several seconds after its process starts before it accepts connections. The web service starts a moment later, tries to connect, and fails.

Docker knows when a process has started. It cannot know by itself when a program is ready to do its job. You have to tell it how to find out.

steps.title: Health checks
steps.text:
A **health check** is a command that Docker runs inside the container at intervals. Exit code 0 means healthy. Anything else means not healthy.

| Setting | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `test` | The command to run. |
| `interval` | How long to wait between checks. |
| `timeout` | How long one check may take before it counts as failed. |
| `retries` | How many failures in a row make the container unhealthy. |
| `start_period` | Time at the start during which failures do not count. |

A container with a health check is `starting`, then `healthy` or `unhealthy`. `docker ps` shows the state.

The command must exist in the image. A good check asks the program a real question, such as whether it accepts a connection, and is cheap enough to run every few seconds.

steps.title: Wait for healthy
steps.text:
With a health check in place, `depends_on` can use its long form and name a condition.

- `service_started` is the default: the container has been started.
- `service_healthy` waits until the health check passes.
- `service_completed_successfully` waits until the container has finished with exit code 0. It suits a one-off job that must run first, such as updating the database's tables.

steps.title: The short form
steps.text:
A Compose file says this, and the `db` service has no health check.

```yaml
  web:
    depends_on:
      - db
```

steps.title: It can still fail later
steps.text:
Start order solves the first minute. It does nothing about the rest of the application's life. A database can restart at three in the morning, long after every `depends_on` was satisfied.

So the real fix belongs in the program: **when a connection fails, wait a little and try again.** A service that retries does not care which container started first.

Use health checks and conditions to make a clean start likely. Do not use them as a reason to skip retrying.

steps.title: Restart policies
steps.text:
A restart policy tells Docker what to do when a container's main process ends.

| Policy | Restarts when |
| --- | --- |
| `no` | Never. This is the default. |
| `on-failure` | The exit code is not 0. |
| `always` | It ends for any reason, and when the Docker daemon starts. |
| `unless-stopped` | As `always`, except after you stopped it yourself. |

`unless-stopped` suits most long-running services. They come back after a crash and after the machine reboots, and stay down when you stop them on purpose.

Docker waits a little longer before each new attempt. And note what a policy does not do: Docker by itself does not restart a container for being **unhealthy**. It restarts one only when the main process ends.

steps.title: Up, down, up, down
steps.text: After a change to its settings, a service looks like this. Each time anyone checks, the uptime is a few seconds.

steps.title: Limits
steps.text:
With no limit, one container can use all of the host's memory and processor time, and starve every other container on the machine.

- A **memory limit** is a hard cap. A container that goes over it is killed by the kernel. It ends with exit code 137, and `docker inspect` reports `OOMKilled: true`.
- A **CPU limit** is a throttle. The container is slowed down and is not killed.

Set a memory limit somewhat above what the service needs in normal use. A leak then takes down one container, which its restart policy brings back, and the rest of the machine carries on.

steps.title: Exercise: a start that works
steps.text:
The tracker has three services: `db`, a one-off `migrate` job that updates the database's tables and exits, and `web`.

1. Describe the order they must become ready in.
2. Write the `depends_on` section of `migrate` and of `web`.
3. Choose a restart policy for each of the three, with a reason.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. `db` must be healthy, then `migrate` must finish successfully, then `web` may start.
2. The sections are below. `web` waits for both. Waiting for `migrate` alone would be enough for the order, and naming `db` too states the real dependency.
3. `db` and `web`: `unless-stopped`, so they return after a crash or a reboot. `migrate`: `no`. It is meant to run once and end. With `always` it would run again and again for ever. If it fails, a person should read why.

questions.prompt: What does this guarantee when `web` starts?

choices.text: That the `db` container has been started
choices.feedback: The short form only orders the starts. The database may still be seconds away from accepting connections.
That needs a health check on `db` and the condition `service_healthy`.
It does order the starts. It does not wait for readiness.

questions.prompt: What is the best next step?

choices.feedback: The policy is doing its job. The program ends with an error each time it starts.
Exit code 1 means the program reported an error, and it does so at every start. The logs say what the new settings broke. Restarting cannot fix a wrong setting.
Running out of memory gives 137. This is exit code 1, an error the program reported itself.
